newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Offshore scramble for future of Taiwan futures.
newsitem.headline: Offshore scramble for future of Taiwan futures.

text.p: A Pacific Rim race for the future of Taiwan's potentially significant futures market begins this week and the only steed not in the gate will be Taiwan's own.

An aggressive, Asia-focussed Chicago Mercantile Exchange had hoped to be first out of the gate at 0100 GMT on January 9 with electronic trading of new futures and futures options contracts linked to Taiwan's stock market performance.
But the CME now is likely to be pipped by the Singapore International Monetary Exchange, or SIMEX, which will launch open-outcry trading of similar Taiwan index contracts a mere five minutes earlier.
San Francisco's venerable Pacific Stock Exchange, bolstering its claim as a U.S. gateway to Asia's financial markets, will begin trading Taiwan stock-index options a day later.

All are defying Taiwan regulators' go-slow appeals in a race to meet what they call intense demand overseas -- and in Taiwan -- for derivatives linked to Taipei's effervescent stock market, one of the world's top 15 in capitalisation and turnover.
Taiwan has no local futures exchange, something long scorned as a gamblers' plaything with little legitimate value. Its stock exchange is unlikely to offer index options before mid-1997.

Playing for time to build a futures infrastructure, Taiwan has stopped short of deeming the rivals hostile but has withheld technical cooperation and threatened to cut off access to stock price data crucial to their indexes.
The fate of Taiwan's planned futures exchange remains a hostage of parliament, still bickering over at least three rival drafts of an enabling Futures Trading Law.
At the same time, Taiwan's watchdog Securities and Exchange Commission has refused to let foreign financial institutions use the local exchange's proprietary TAIEX index.
Nor has it legalised trading of offshore Taiwan index futures by Taiwan brokerages or investors, who are expected to skirt the ban by opening "underground" accounts offshore.

Analysts say local investors, who can legally trade overseas commodities futures, have legitimate need of a stock market hedge. Experts estimate Taiwan stock-index futures could fuel T$50 billion (US$1.8 billion) a month in first-year turnover.
The securities commission on Saturday announced a half-year grace period during which it would monitor the offshore rivals but not interfere with their operations.

But it reiterated its right to cut off real-time stock price data to Dow Jones and Co's Taiwan index, to be used by the Merc and Pacific exchange, and one compiled by a Morgan Stanley group unit that underlies the SIMEX contracts.
"We will at least wait a period of six months to evaluate whether to do so or to legalise their products," agency chairman Lu Tung-ying Lu said in a statement.
Dow Jones and Morgan Stanley both say their Taiwan indexes have extremely high correlations to the local exchange's TAIEX.

Most alarmingly for eager would-be investors in Taiwan, Lu announced a new delay for the local futures exchange, saying parliament's failure to adopt a draft Futures Trading Law in 1996 meant an exchange could not open before 1998.
In a mid-1996 bout of optimism, regulators said competition could spur a launch as early as July 1997 but they later said the legislative impasse would delay the exchange to October.
Despite the ban on local trading of offshore futures, Taiwan regulators have not acted to block real-time data about them.
